The delegates suspect that the competitor's prior attempt (DNF) was a result of the competitor going over the time limit, and the unsolved cube was sent back to the scramble table, where it was mistakenly perceived as scrambled by a runner. 

The WRC agreed that the attempt should be ruled as a DNF.

entries.title: Competitor claimed misscramble after round but video footage was unclear
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since the resolution of this incident, the regulation [11i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i) has been updated to provide stricter criteria for when a misscramble should receive an extra.

After the conclusion of a round, a competitor looked at the scrambles they were supposed to receive and reported to have gotten a misscramble. There was a video recording of the solve, but it was very poor footage, and it was unclear whether or not the scramble was correct based solely on the footage. The delegates decided to provide a provisional extra.

The WRC reviewed the footage and were also unable to determine whether or not the scramble was correct. As a result, the ruling was to rely on delegate discretion - delegates should make the decision based on their interactions with a competitor, and give an extra if they believe it is more likely that the competitor received a misscramble.

entries.title: 3x3x3 With Feet solving with a non-official Stackmat
entries.content: One competitor was found to be using a non-official Stackmat timer, which wasn't provided by the organization team for the 3x3x3 With Feet event, and it was granted an extra attempt. It was decided that the organization team is responsible to provide the competition equipment, and the result of the extra attempt was accepted.

entries.title: Clock not fully intact at end of attempt
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since the resolution of this incident, regulation [10h1a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#10h1a) has been introduced to clearly define how these incidents should be handled.

Upon ending an attempt, a competitor's clock "exploded" in place. Some of the screws holding the puzzle together had come undone, and the plastic framing was noticeably out of its home position. The puzzle was clearly solved (supported by the intact, complete backside), but the pieces were not assembled correctly.

After reviewing picture evidence, the WRC ruled the puzzle to be in a solved state, citing Regulation 5b5f to make the decision. If one were to put the plastic casing of the puzzle back together in the closest position to where it was, all of the dials of the clock would be pointing to the noon position.

entries.title: Qiyi timer used for official attempts
entries.content:
A competition was found to have used a Qiyi timer for official attempts. The delegate supplied a list of competitors' attempts that were done on the Qiyi timer, however, it was unclear if this list was complete and had correctly enumerated all of the affected attempts.

Considering that there was likely a large amount of official solves done on the timer, it would be quite difficult to discern exactly which solvers were done using it. Consequently, due to the lack of confidence in the exact solves that were affected, it would not be fair to DNF/remove some results and not others.

In a decision that was not taken lightly, the WRC decided to remove all results from the competition. Please note that this decision falls in line with precedent such as [this incident.](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/79)

entries.title: Judge briefly touched puzzle before conclusion of attempt
entries.content:
A competitor had dropped their clock before stopping the timer and the judge interfered and touched the clock before the competitor picked it up and completed the attempt.

While the judge's reasonable attempt to verify if the puzzle was indeed solved may have briefly prevented the competitor from picking up the clock again, the negative impact of the competitor not stopping the timer correctly outweighs any disadvantage caused by the judge's interference. As a result, the original attempt is kept.

entries.title: Competitor was distracted by another competitor and simultaneously faced a timer issue
entries.content:
During a competitor's pyraminx attempt, a different competitor began talking to them. The affected competitor, upon completing their attempt, called for a delegate to request an extra. However, the timer display showed 0.000. The affected competitor claimed that due to habit, they had immediately reset the timer after their solve. However, a judge mentioned that they heard the competitor mention that they had not started the timer upon completion of the solve. 

This is a particularly complex situations because of two incidents occurring in tandem: the distraction from the other competitor, and the timer situation. It was unclear the extent of the distraction by the other competitor as well as when the distraction occurred (i.e. during inspection, in the midst of the very short solve, etc). 

In general, if two incidents occur during the same attempt, the incident that occurred first takes precedence. In this situation, it was not possible to determine for certain which incident occurred first. If the distraction occurred during inspection, then the ordering of incidents would be known.  Due to the lack of information the WRC had regarding the magnitude and duration of the distraction, the decision was left to delegate discretion, suggesting that if the distraction started during inspection and was significant, then an extra could be used. Otherwise, the penalty should be a DNF. In the end, the result was marked as a DNF.

entries.title: Pyraminx round affected by a great amount of misscrambles
entries.content:
After a competition had ended, a delegate received messages from two of the pyraminx solvers indicating that their scrambles for the first round of pyraminx were almost entirely wrong. Between the two competitors, only 3 out of 10 scrambles they received were correct, with the remaining being off by a tip (both direction and quantity) or scrambled in the wrong orientation.

The WRC made the tough decision to remove the affected Pyraminx round. Given the high misscramble rate and the very limited videographic evidence available to check, ensuring that scrambles were equal in difficulty for all competitors would be nearly impossible. As a result, the decision was to remove the affected round, which would ultimately mean removing all rounds of Pyraminx.

entries.title: Round re-run after scrambles were found to be "incorrectly" generated
entries.content:
After a round of 6x6 and 7x7 had concluded, the staff found that the scrambles were generated under "manual mode" with TNoodle. They thought that this made the round invalid and decided to re-run the rounds. 

While it is typically simpler to generate scramble sets for a selected competition in TNoodle, there is no prohibition against using manual mode. As a result, it was encouraged to use the original results. However, these scorecards were discarded during the competition, as the organizers and delegates believed that they would be invalid. Therefore, the results of the "re-run" rounds of 6x6 and 7x7 were used.

entries.title: Competitor faced a sequence of misscrambles
entries.content: A competitor was caught in a frenzy of misplaced scrambles and cubes, receiving a different cube on one occasion and a particular scramble more than once. The competitor DNFed two attempts, which gave them the impression that they would DNF the average. However, it was noticed after the round that one of these was actually a duplicate scramble, which meant that it wasn’t fair to retain the DNF on it. Since they could still get an average on the remaining solves that were originally DNSed by them, the WRC decided under [11d ](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11d)that it was best to leave this to delegate discretion in the pretext of fair sportsmanship. The solves were re-ordered appropriately and the remaining attempts were granted back to the competitor under such unique circumstances.

entries.title: Delegate awarded themselves an extra attempt after attempt had concluded
entries.content: A delegate at this competition was competing and received another competitor’s cube on a 4x4 solve. While the delegate wasn’t distracted by this, he realized and decided to grant himself an extra after the solve, resetting the timer immediately before it was recorded by the judge. There was a split opinion amongst the other delegates at this competition as to whether this warranted the extra, since another competitor also had a similar issue but didn’t receive an extra on account of not being distracted. While the WRC decided to leave this up to delegate discretion, we strongly advised that the original attempt (in this case, DNF) be kept, as the competitor did not request an extra until the solve was complete (see 11e+++)

entries.title: Competitor used visibly broken headphones during attempt
entries.content: A competitor was found to be wearing headphones while competing. The headphones were disconnected and were clearly broken (the competitor had cut the headphone cables). The WRC decided to keep the result, indicating that headphones that are clearly broken can be considered non-electronic for the purposes of 2i. As a kind reminder, disconnected headphones are NOT allowed if they still have electronic parts (see [2i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i))

entries.title: Delegate accidentally reused scrambles from previous competition
entries.content:
The delegate of [ERAU Speedcubing Spring 2018](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/competitions/ERAUSpeedcubingSpring2018) accidentally used scrambles from a prior competition ([STEM Educ8 2018](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/competitions/STEMEduc82018)) for multiple rounds of this competition. These scrambles have been publicly accesible since the results of the earlier competition were published.

The WRC has decided that all affected results of ERAU Speedcubing Spring 2018 will not be accepted as official WCA results. These are: 2x2x2 Cube, 3x3x3 Cube, 4x4x4 Cube, 3x3x3 One-Handed, Pyraminx and Square-1.
Accordingly, only the results of Megaminx and 7x7x7 Cube will be recognized.

We know that this is a harsh decision with consequences for many young competitors. However, the integrity of scrambles in WCA competitions is essential and does not allow us to be lenient here.

entries.title: Competitor and judge were unsure of when timer was stopped
entries.content:
Towards the end of an attempt, a competitor dropped their puzzle and went to stop the timer, then realized that the puzzle wasn't yet solved and went to fix the puzzle (by applying one move) and then stopping the timer. The judge was unsure of if the timer was stopped on the competitor's first or second attempt of stopping the timer. A provisional extra was granted.

The WRC ruled to leave this incident up to delegate discretion. If the judge and delegate are both unsure about what had happened, then it is recommended to use an extra.

entries.title: Timer flipped over during an attempt
entries.content:
A competitor started their solve as per usual, but the timer came loose, flipped over and landed upside-down on the mat. The competitor proceeded to finish their solve before placing the timer back in position and stopping it. The competitor seemed to have been disadvantaged by an equipment malfunction through no fault of their own. A provisional extra was given.

As a reminder, from regulation 11e:
> [11e](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11e)) ...The competitor should appeal verbally or in writing to the judge and WCA Delegate at the time of the incident, before finishing the original attempt, to be eligible for an extra attempt...

Although competitors should appeal when an incident occurs, the incident happened during Skewb, a quick event, and the impact of the timer movement may not have been apparent until the competitor tried to stop the timer. Competition Delegates are best placed to assess the overall evidence available in this case. Thus, situations like this are left to Delegate discretion, with an extra attempt being the recommendation.

entries.title: Competitor believed time noted down was faster than actuality
entries.content:
After a competitor had completed their Skewb average, they approached a delegate and mentioned that their second solve of 6.52 was incorrectly written, and should have instead been a 7.52. The time on the scoresheet was indeed written as 6.52 and was signed off by both the competitor and judge. No video was available of this attempt. During discussion, the competitor began second-guessing their memory and became increasingly unsure of what the actual time was. In the moment, a provisional extra was given.

The WRC advises **not** to use an extra attempt, and to leave the decision of whether the time should be 6.52 or 7.52 up to *delegate discretion*. Making such a decision is dependent on assessing all of the available evidence, and competition delegates are often best suited for this. It is worth noting that a potentially unreliable memory is not very strong evidence on its own.

entries.title: Delegate started scrambling for a group they were to compete in
entries.content:
A delegate was doing table management at the start of a group when they decided to help out scrambling the first couple of cubes because many judges were already waiting at the scrambling table. After scrambling a few cubes, the delegate realized that they themselves were supposed to compete in the current group. After consulting with another delegate, they decided to not generate a new set of scrambles, but instead give the delegate that was to compete E1, as they had only seen the first scramble.

Scrambles must not be visible to competitors ([WSAP](https://documents.worldcubeassociation.org/documents/policies/external/Scramble%20Accountability.pdf) 5.1.1), and if competitors are required to act as scrambles for their own group, they must be prevented from seeing any scrambles they have not yet attempted ([1h1](https://wcaregs.netlify.app/#1h1)). By scrambling some cubes and having access to the scrambling document, the delegate did have the opportunity to see all scrambles of the group. In accordance with maintaining scramble secrecy requirements, the WRC concluded that all results from the average must be removed. Delegates are considered highly trustworthy and have specific responsibilities for handling scrambles. However, when they act in a competitor role, scramble secrecy requirements applying to competitors must still apply to them.

entries.title: Pyraminx tip caps partially detached when determining misalignment penalties
entries.content:
A competitor finished their pyraminx solve and had one of the tips misaligned with caps not fully intact:

![](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/rails/active_storage/blobs/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6NDcwNTksInB1ciI6ImJsb2JfaWQifX0=--b9956b3a663b0bf0a0d839d39b5352e91feba702/Screenshot%202024-11-18%20at%203.08.47%E2%80%AFPM.png)

Two of the pieces that construct the pyraminx tip were slightly separated. The third piece was intact, and with respect to this piece, the delegates determined that the piece was turned less than 60 degrees.

In this case, the puzzle was determined to be solved. In incidents like this, the misalignment should be judged by the piece that is intact (as the delegates did) rather than any partially detatched pieces. 

As a friendly reminder: for some incidents similar to this, regulation [5b5c](https://wcaregs.netlify.app/#5b5c) may need to be applied. In this particular incident, the affected pieces were only minorly displaced and partially detatched, so the critical pieces are considered intact following [5b5f](https://wcaregs.netlify.app/#5b5f).

entries.title: Competitor received two identical scrambles on a 2-cube MBLD attempt
entries.content:
A competitor attempted 2 puzzles in an attempt of multi-blind. A scrambling mistake was made such that both cubes got the same scramble. The competitor continued with their attempt and only reported the mistake after the attempt. However, the delegates of the competition were doing MBLD attempts themselves at this time. Because of this, an extra attempt was granted to the competitor by the judge. 

Citing 1c, it was ruled that using the extra attempt granted by the judge (in lieu of the delegates) was fine to use, as this regulation allows for delegates to appoint responsibilities to other people. 

As a general reminder to delegates and organizers, if all delegates are competing at the same time, a specific individual should be prior appointed to have oversight and be in charge of giving out extras if necessary. 

As a reminder for competitors: if facing a similar situation of encountering duplicate scrambles in a multiblind attempt, bring this up to the delegates/organizers/judges immediately instead of proceeding with the attempt.

entries.title: Competitor with excessive sweating unable to stop timer
entries.content:
A competitor with a condition experiences excessive sweating on the palms of their hands. Due to the nature of timers, excessive sweat on the hands can require the competitor to stop the timer with more force or attempting multiple times to stop the timer. In this case, the timer would not stop due to the excessive moisture on the sensors. The delegate were familiar with the competitor and their condition, and in this incident, granted an extra attempt. 

The WRC ruled that the decision to give an extra attempt was entirely reasonable. 

Competitors who experience a similar condition should contact their delegate *prior* to a competition to seek accommodations, per [2s](https://wcaregs.netlify.app/#2s). A possible accommodation can be stopping the timer with the back of the hands -- however, this should only be done after a delegate approves of this behavior.

entries.title: Competitor's scorecard went missing
entries.content:
A competitor competed in the 3x3 OH event, but later recognized that their results had not been entered. After searching the venue, the scorecard remained missing. The competitor was not suspected of deliberately misplacing their scorecard, so after discussion amongst delegates, it was agreed to grant the competitor provisional extra attempts. The competitor initially preferred to have their results marked as a DNS, but later agreed to complete the extra attempts.

The WRC ruled that since the provisional extras were completed *at the competition*, the extras must be used. If there were no results available, then a DNS would have been appropriate.

As an important note: if a competitor's scorecard goes missing at no fault of their own, then they are entitled to an extra, and one should be provided. Competitors then have the option of choosing to complete these extras or to DNS them.

entries.title: Competitor received incorrect order of scrambles
entries.content:
During a round of 7x7, a competitor was mistakenly given scramble 2 for their first attempt. The competitor did not make cutoff. Realizing the mistake, the competitor was given scramble 1 provisionally, and also did not make cutoff. 

As would be done with swapped scrambles in a non-cutoff round, the results have to be rearranged, so the result of the attempt with scramble 1 was kept as the only recorded result.

entries.title: Competitor reset timer after signing a different scorecard
entries.content:
The delegates of a competition discovered a missing signature for a competitor's scorecard for another event while they were competing in 3x3 One-Handed. After the competitor finished their solve, the delegate approached them, prompting them to add the missing signature. The competitor then reset their timer before the judge was able to write down the time for the current attempt. A provisional extra was given for this attempt.

The WRC voted to have the result for this attempt be a DNF, as having signed the other scorecard is unrelated to their actual solve. The competitor is responsible for resetting the timer in this incident, and A6f1 is clear about the penalty.

entries.title: Irregular enforcement of time limits for 3x3x3 Multiple Blindfolded
entries.content:
At Kansai Open 2018, 3x3x3 Multi-Blind was held as "Best of 2" with a cumulative time limit in combination with the regular time limit. The WCA Guidelines clarify it is not possible to hold 3x3x3 Multi-Blind with a cumulative time limit.

The WRC has decided that all results of the second attempt should be removed. This decision only affected one comeptitor (all other results were DNS).

entries.title: Tripod fell on competitor during inspection and stopped attempt
entries.content:
During inspection, a competitor's tripod fell on them. The competitor stopped the solve, thinking it was a DNF since they believed they could not touch their phone (as was a previous rule). Under newer regulations, putting the tripod back in place would not have disqualified the solve. The competitor was granted a provisional extra.

The WRC ruled that given regulation 2t, the competitor is reponsible for being familiar with the newest version of the WCA regulations before competing. Therefore, this incident is at the fault of the competitor, and the attempt was ruled a DNF.

entries.title: Scorecards misplaced and later found, removing competitor from round
entries.content:
Two competitors, competitor X and competitor Y, were both vying for a spot in the final round. Their round 1 results were very close, with competitor X beating out competitor Y, and the competitors took their scorecards aside to do their own calculations before the scores were properly entered. Somewhere along this process, the scorecards were misplaced and could not be found.

The delegates lines up a clear set of circumstances for a procedure: The competitors would redo the first round on a new set of scrambles to determine who would go to the final. The new results would not stand if the original scorecards turned up, and if the "wrong" person competed in the final, then neither of them would advance. These circumstances are in line with [Regulation 9t](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#9t). The competitors agreed to this, and in these new attempts, competitor Y was faster and was placed in the final.

Much later, after the rounds, the original scorecards were found. Since the delegates and competitors had agreed on a procedure, competitor Y's results were removed from the final. Note that competitor X did not have any results for the final at all.

The competitors were at fault for misplacing their scoresheets, and since the delegates had laid out a complete plan of actions, the WRC agreed that it was best to stick to the delegate decision. The WRC recommends in similar situations that both competitors compete in the final provisionally if at all possible.

entries.title: Question mark written on scorecard
entries.content:
The time written on a scorecard appeared as "57.?". The delegates tried locating the judge and competitor for the attempt, but were unable to get a response. The competitor was emailed after the competition asking what happened, but no response was given. 

The delegates made the assumption that the question mark on the scorecard meant that the timer was reset by either the competitor or judge before the time was written down. 

The WRC agrees with the decision to record this result as a DNF. One possible explanation of what occurred during this attempt is indeed that the competitor reset the timer prematurely, and this situation is not unlikely, thus, under A7c+, the result should be a DNF.

entries.title: Competitor started the timer improperly, only visible with frame-by-frame video analysis
entries.content:
Many instances of results where timers were started in ways that violated Regulation A4b and/or Regulation A4b1 were discovered, but were not visible when viewing footage at full speed.

A4b) The competitor uses their fingers to touch the elevated sensor surfaces of the Stackmat timer. The competitor's palms must be facing down, and located on the side of the timer that is closer to the competitor. Penalty: time penalty (+2 seconds).
A4b1) The competitor must have no physical contact with the puzzle while starting the solve. Penalty: time penalty (+2 seconds).

Previously, the WRC only viewed footage at full speed to determine penalties, based on [this incident](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/50). After further discussion, the WRC decided to change its approach to use frame-by-frame analysis to determine penalties on certain results as described [here](https://forum.worldcubeassociation.org/t/wrc-statement-on-frame-by-frame-analysis/55294), and with the permission of the WCA Board of Directors, to do so retroactively on past results. As a result, the WRC analyzed various results and applied the corresponding penalties to applicable cases.

The approach used by WRC to analyze timer starts in this case can be seen as follows:
1. The video’s frame rate is determined, and the time of the attempt in frames is calculated and rounded up (Example: 0.74 Seconds = 44.4 frames, rounded up to 45 frames @ 60 FPS).
2. The first frame in which the timer could have been stopped is determined. If there are two frames where the timer could have been stopped (i.e. the stop likely happened in between two frames), the earlier frame is selected. At least two members must confirm the timer stop frame.
3.  The video is rewound by the number of frames calculated in step 1. The frame that the video ends up on after the rewind is considered the timer start and used as a basis to analyze for penalties. At least two members must confirm the timer start frame.
4.  A penalty is only applied if the WRC strongly believes that a violation of the Regulation(s) occurred. This is determined through a vote.

For more details regarding the affected attempts, please see [this announcement](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/posts/wrc-decisions-with-frame-by-frame-analysis) on the final WRC decision.
 
The WCA Regulations will be updated to reflect this change in the WRC’s approach.

entries.title: Competitor turned the puzzle before the judge had clearly inspected it
entries.content:
After a solve, a competitor picked up their puzzle and began to turn it again while the judge was recording the result. No penalty was issued by the judge. Competition Delegates subsequently reviewed video footage of the attempt and chose to disqualify (DNF) the result based on Regulation [A6e1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A6e1), as the judge had not clearly inspected the puzzle before the competitor began to turn it in again. When Delegates later spoke to the judge, he confirmed the puzzle was solved before recording the result.

The WRC chose to remove the DNF penalty. While the judge had not clearly inspected the puzzle, the attempt had moved past the point at which the puzzle would be subject to inspection and it was reasonable for the competitor to pick up and turn their puzzle at the time they did.

While video evidence demonstrated that the puzzle was solved, the WRC did not consider this relevant to this decision. Regulation [A6e](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A6e) requires the judge to inspect the puzzle, rather than being based on the puzzle's state. In this case the video evidence for the judge inspecting the puzzle was inconclusive, but the other factors described above drove the WRC's overall decision. If video demonstrating a solved state could be used to override [A6e](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A6e) then this could lead to an undesirable increase in workload for Delegates and the WRC from assessing such videos.

entries.title: 2x2 misscramble took only 3 moves to solve
entries.content:
A video was found where a competitor could be seen performing a 0.54 2x2 Solve, this being the North American Record at that time. After some analysis, it was determined that the cube was in fact misscrambled, with a 3 move optimal solution (R U R’), rather than the intended 4 move optimal solution (U’ R U R’).

The optimal solution for any official 2x2 scrambles has a minimum of 4 moves ([Regulation 4b3b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b3b)). The WRC held a vote to confirm our decision to DNF the attempt, in line with our approach for handling misscrambles at the time.

If this were to happen under the current Regulations, the solve would be marked as DNS as per [Regulation 11i1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i1).

entries.title: Competitor got a DNF result on a timer that was not reset
entries.content:
A competitor did not solve their puzzle successfully in 3x3x3 Blindfolded. After their attempt was completed it was noticed that the attempt was performed on a timer that had not been reset.

WRC decided that the events in this incident should be evaluated in the order in which they happened, with earlier violations taking precedence over later ones. Since the judge failed to reset the timer (a violation of B2a) before the competitor attempted to stop the timer with an unsolved puzzle, an extra should be granted to the competitor, even if during their attempt the competitor was not aware that their timer was not running.

If an extra would only be granted if the first attempt was a success, the competitor would have to get two successful results in a row to get a non-DNF result.

entries.title: Competitor checked if camera was on during inspection
entries.content:
During inspection, the competitor looked to see if his camera was recording. To do this, he stood up and looked at the screen of his phone, before sitting back down and starting the solve. This behavior could be considered a violation of regulation [2i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#2i), but it was unclear if the competitor's behavior qualified as "using" an electronic device. 

The WRC concluded that the result should stand without penalty, citing the following reasons:
1. Regulation 2i2 allows for restricted use of cameras by the competitor, as clarified in 2i2a and 2i2c.
2. 2i2a clarifies that delegate discretion can be used to determine whether or not a competitor gained an advantage from electronic usage.
3. 2i2c prohibits the competitor from pressing any buttons on electronics, which did not occur in this incident.

It was determined that since the competitor was just checking to see if their camera was on and recording, they did not gain an advantage or receive assistance by looking at the camera.

entries.title: Several issues with the venue setup
entries.content:
There were several issues and concerns regarding the venue setup at this competition. The main point was that waiting competitors were able to watch competing competitors. Additionally, it was obviously possible to choose scramble groups by cutting the waiting line.

The questionable setup was reported by a competitor who intentionally tried to abuse it by pre-inspecting scrambles in one round. The WRC agreed with him to change all his results from this particular round to DNF.

entries.title: Competitor stopped timer with potential karate chop
entries.content:
During a final round, a delegate was watching the competitors' solves in case any incident occurred. The delegate observed a competitor who stopped the timer in a "karate chop" position, and went to tell the judge to apply a +2 penalty. Afterwards, the delegate was presented with the video of the attempt from the competitor, and the competitor claimed that the +2 was incorrectly given. While watching the video at normal speed, the timer stop still looked illegal, but in slow motion it was *slightly* more debatable. 

The WRC agreed that the timer stop violated A6d when viewing the video at full speed. As an important clarification, the frame-by-frame policy as outlined in [11f](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11f) can be used to remove a penalty initially assessed by the judge or delegate ([11f1d](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11f1d)), however, applying a penalty must only be based on evidence viewed at full speed (unless the solve falls within the scope of [11f1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11f1)).

entries.title: Judge did not reset timer and recorded the previous competitor's time
entries.content:
A competitor unknowingly performed their first solve without resetting the timer, which displayed a time from a previous attempt. The incorrect time was recorded on the scorecard. Upon review, it was noticed that the result seemed unusual. After consulting with the competitor and their parent, a video confirmed the actual time was significantly different. Since the exact time couldn't be verified, the result was changed to a DNF, which was accepted by the competitor and their parent.

The WRC concluded that the delegate could have decided to give the competitor an extra instead of a DNF. Since the main problem in this incident was the judge not resetting the timer ([A3b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A3b)), the delegate could have decided to give the competitor an extra attempt instead of a DNF if the incident was found out about on time ([A3c3+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A3c3+)). Though the competitor is allowed to reset the timer themselves, this is ultimately the judge's responsibility. The WRC would like to remind judges to be mindful of the state of their timer when judging and to ensure their station is ready for the next attempt.

entries.title: Competitor likely received a misscramble on a National Record attempt
entries.content:
A competitor had broken the National Record single in Skewb, which was significantly faster than their average in the event. Due to the cheering and excitement, the delegate and competitor were only able to meet at the end of the competition to verify the scramble. After multiple attempts, the competitor claimed that they were unfamiliar with the true scramble (that they were supposed to receive)

The competitor was then encouraged to try out the scramble at home once scrambles were posted, but the competitor asked for help in reading the notation, which lead to suspicion regarding the validity of the record. The delegate also noticed that the scorecard for the record-breaking attempt was not signed by the scrambler. Due to all of these factors, there was high suspicion that the cube was incorrectly scrambled.

The WRC agreed that the cube was likely not scrambled correctly, and ruled that the incident should be handled assuming that the scramble was not correct. Following [11i1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11i1), since no extra attempt was given at the competition, the attempt was ruled as a DNS. 

In order to reduce the penalties that must be given to competitors who receive incorrectly scrambled puzzles, the WRC recommends the following:
- Competitors who are expected to meet the crieteria in [11i1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11i1) should have their scrambles checked by a second scrambler ([11i1+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11i1+))
- Competitors who achieve results meeting the criteria in [11i1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11i1) should have their scrambles checked as soon as is reasonable.
- Provisional extras can be given if the resolution to an incident is unclear in the moment. ([11e+++++](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11e+++++))

entries.title: Competitor realized the color scheme on their puzzle was swapped during their solve
entries.content:
A competitor in the Square-1 final round requested an extra attempt after realizing that a friend had swapped the top and bottom colors on their puzzle, altering the color scheme. This resulted in his solve being a DNF with the top and bottom layers being swapped, as a direct result of this modification. The competitor acknowledged that they had submitted the puzzle themselves but was unaware of this modification at that time. They made sure not to sign their time before calling over the Delegate.

The WRC concluded that, even though it was the competitor's own puzzle that he handed in himself, not having knowledge of such a modification can cause a significant amount of distraction. That, combined with the fact the attempt wasn't signed for yet, makes it so that the extra was warranted by [11d](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#11d), considering that the DNF was a direct result of the swapped colors. 

In cases like this, Delegates should use reasonable discretion to determine the most fair outcome. Had the competitor known about their color scheme being swapped, it would not be as reasonable to grant the extra attempt.

entries.title: Competitor thought timer malfunctioned after getting second DNF for timer start
entries.content:
A competitor called a delegate over after getting a second DNF because the timer did not start. This was a very experienced competitor, and had no explanation as to why this happened. The competitor believed they held their hands on the timer long enough, but the judge was unsure if the green starting light was visible or not. 

The delegates tested the timers that were used on the two DNF attempts and had no issues with them, and nobody else complained about the timers for the rest of the competition. Videos of the solves were provided for analysis. 

The WRC reviewed the information and videos and concluded that the DNFs should be kept. The competitor had a tendency of starting the timer quite fast (even on successful starts), and on the DNF attempts, their hands were held on the timer for a bit less time, justifying why the timer did not start. Additionally, since there were no other complaints about the timer during the competition, it is very likely that the competitor simply did not start the timer correctly. As a result, both attempts remained as DNFs.

entries.title: Competitor started a Multiblind attempt without a judge present
entries.content:
A competitor began their 3x3x3 Multi-blind attempt without a judge present, assuming they could start with a stackmat timer due to the use of floating judges. Realizing their mistake, the competitor asked if their attempt should be a DNF. When the delegate told them that this was the case they stopped their attempt. After reconsideration however, the delegates provided a provisional extra attempt.

The WRC clarified that starting a blindfolded attempt without a judge violates regulation [B2a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#B2a), which states that a judge must be present at the start of each attempt. Furthermore, a stopwatch should have been started as required by Regulation [A1b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A1b) since the time limit was over 10 minutes. Since the competitor's actions prevented proper judging, the WRC ruled that the original attempt should be disqualified (DNF).

entries.title: Missing signatures from the judge and competitor, video evidence was available but the judge could not be located
entries.content:
A score sheet was found missing both signatures. Video evidence confirmed the attempt, and the competitor acknowledged it, but the judge could not be located. Initially, organizers mistakenly believed the competitor was a newcomer and provisionally allowed the result, uncertain if [A7c8](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A7c8) permitted video evidence to replace the judge’s signature. After realizing the competitor was not a newcomer, they considered changing the result to DNF and sought WRC confirmation.

The WRC clarified that if this were to involve an inexperienced competitor, [Regulation A7c8](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A7c8) allows a judge to add their signature later, but only if they can still be contacted. It is not permitted for anyone to sign on behalf of the judge. In this incident, the fact that the judge was unable to be located meant that the signature could not be added anymore. Furthermore, the competitor in question turned out not to be a newcomer after all, meaning that A7c8 did not apply anymore. All of this resulted in the WRC deciding that this result should be changed to a DNF.

entries.title: Competitor entered the scramble area after scrambling started, but before his first solve
entries.content:
A competitor submitted their puzzle and went to the waiting area but then entered the scrambling area, mistakenly believing their puzzle had been swapped. They saw their puzzle with the first scramble, leading to a DNF for that attempt. Uncertain about the correct penalty, the delegates asked if only the first attempt should be disqualified or if the entire average should be affected.

The WRC clarified that violating [A2a1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A2a1) allows for the disqualification of all remaining attempts at the delegate's discretion. Additionally, entering the scrambling area early violated [A2a3](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A2a3), which, while not listing a specific penalty, could justify round disqualification under [2k5](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#2k5). Since this occurred before any solves were completed, the competitor should receive no results rather than DNFs ([2j1a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#2j1a)).

The WRC would like to give a reminder that competitors must never enter the scrambling area while scrambling is in progress, as scramble secrecy must be maintained throughout the group.

entries.title: Competitor mistakenly reported duplicate scramble in Square-1
entries.content:
A competitor reported that he had received the same scrambles for the first and second attempt in Square-1. It turned out that both attempts were scrambled correctly so the result of the second attempt was initially recorded as DNF but an extra attempt was granted.

As both cube shapes were indeed similar, the WRC has decided to accept the result of the extra attempt to acknowledge the honesty of the competitor and to avoid discouraging competitors from reporting repeated scrambles.

entries.title: Competitor got a time below 0.06 because of shaky hands
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since the resolution of this incident, [A6b1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#A6b1) has been changed, to better state how incidents with a timer stop under 0.06s should be handled.

A competitor got a timer stop with a time less than 0.06s. An extra was given for malfunctioning equipment, but the judge said it could have been the competitors fault because of shaking hands.

The WRC determined that the most likely reason were the shaky hands of the competitor and that the result should therefore be DNF'ed, in accordance with A6b1, because the cause was not a timer malfunction:

> A6b1) If the timer stops before the competitor has solved the puzzle and the timer shows a time strictly below 0.06 seconds, then the attempt is replaced by an extra attempt. A competitor forfeits the right to the additional attempt if the WCA Delegate determines that the timer was stopped deliberately.

After an appeal to the WRC Board, the Board decided to overturn the decision by the WRC, citing that shaking hands do not count as stopping the timer **deliberately**. The DNF was therefore changed to the time of the extra solve.

entries.title: Staff member competes in missed rounds without knowledge of Delegate and organizer
entries.content:
A competitor was late for the first round of 4x4x4 and 5x5x5. He asked the organizer if it would still be possible to compete, which  was denied. As the competitor was also a staff member, he decided to ask a fellow staff member to scramble and judge his attempts.

The WRC has decided that the results of both rounds must be removed. The competitor abused his position as a staff member and got a preferential treatment through this. This was also a violation of [4b4](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b4) as the scrambles had already been used earlier.

entries.title: Competitor filmed his attempts with a front-facing camera
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since resolution of this incident, regulation [2i2a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i2a) has been updated to allow for delegate discretion for this type of incident.

A competitor used a front-facing camera in the first round of 2x2x2. This was noticed before the 3rd attempt. He admitted he had used the same camera setup in the previous rounds.
The WRC decided to DNF the previous results per [2i2a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i2a)

entries.title: Missing signatures found after the competition
entries.content:
Both the competitor's and the judge's signatures were found missing for one attempt in Skewb after the competition. The WRC decided to change the result to DNF.

This incident is violating and ignoring [A7b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7b) and [A7c](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7c). More concrete, the judge did not acknowledge that the result is correct, complete, properly formatted, and clearly readable and the competitor did not check and sign the result. These are the steps to finish an attempt.

Although this can be seen as a harsh decision, we believe that these are important regulations to assure the correctness and validness result. For that reason, accepting results which were done without following [A7b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7b) and [A7c](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7c), should not be accepted as valid results.

entries.title: A competitor used one cube with a logo in a Multi-Blind attempt
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: As of 2025, there is now a clear regulation, regulation [3k2b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3k2b), that states that cubes with a logo during multiblind should count as unsolved. 

A competitor used a cube with a logo in his Multi-Blind attempt. This was only found after the attempt.
Currently, according to [3k2](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3k2), using a non-permitted puzzle results in DNF of the attempt. As this would be a very harsh consequence in Multi-Blind, the WRC has decided count the non-permitted puzzle as unsolved, without affecting other puzzles
The WRC is discussing how to revise the Regulations to reflect this policy (see [GitHub issue](https://github.com/thewca/wca-regulations/issues/545)).

entries.title: A judge sent the cube back to the scrambling table before the competitor could sign
entries.content:
In the final round of Skewb, a competitor received a good result and reacted excitedly. While he was inattentive for a short moment, his judge did not write the result down but sent the puzzle back to the scrambling table. This was discovered when the competitor realized he didn't sign for the attempt. A provisional extra attempt was granted at the competition.

The WRC has decided that the original result should be kept. The judge did not follow the approach described in the Regulations. More specifically, he ignored [A7b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7b) by not recording the result. We believe that this should not result in a disadvantage for the competitor. Furthermore, there was enough proof that the original result was legit (recordings as well as eyewitnesses).

entries.title: A judge forgot to hold a sheet between the competitor's face and the puzzle (extra available)
entries.content:
*DISCLAIMER*: After these incidents took place, [B4c](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#B4c) has been changed to explicitly state that in similar incidents the original solve can stand, if the delegate believes the competitor didn't have any bad intentions

A judge forgot to hold a sheet between the competitor's face and the puzzle. This was found after the end of the attempt and a provisional extra was granted.
The WRC decided to accept the result as there was no sign of the competitor abusing the situation and it was not his fault.


The same situation occurred during PBQ Berkeley 2018 where the original attempt was kept.

For a lot of incidents, the WRC used the reasoning that it's better to use an extra attempt where the procedure was correctly followed over an existing attempt where there was a problem with the procedure.
The WRC used this reasoning for PBQ Oshawa 2019, where an extra was available and used over the existing attempt.

entries.title: 3x3x3 One-Handed Attempt was identified as misscramble
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since the resolution of this incident, the regulation [11i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i) has been updated. The outcome of this incident wouldn't change, but how it should be handled is now explicitely stated in the regulations. 

A competitor broke the European Record in his fourth attempt the second round of 3x3x3 One-Handed. When trying to reconstruct the solve, it was discovered that the puzzle was not scrambled correctly (one move in the middle of the scramble was missing). The competitor was granted a provisional extra attempt at the competition.

The WRC decided to replace the original attempt with the extra attempt.

entries.title: A competitor briefly touched the puzzle immediately after stopping the timer
entries.content:
In 4x4x4, first round, a competitor got excited about his result and briefly touched the puzzle immediately after stopping the timer.

Since the touch was unintentional, the solve will not be penalized. The A6e rule will be updated to comply with this ruling.

entries.title: Old version of TNoodle used for Pyraminx scrambles
entries.content:
While re-generating scrambles for the 1st round of Pyraminx to accommodate a larger number of competitor groups, the Delegate accidentally used a version of TNoodle from 3 years ago (0.9.0). This version of TNoodle generates a different distribution of Pyraminx scrambles from the current version (0.13.3). Although it is unclear if this could have had a significant impact on competitors in this particular case, there is no general way to decide whether competitors may have received an advantage in an incident like this. As a result, the WRC has decided that [Regulation 4f](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4f) applies to this incident without exception, invalidating results from affected people in the first round of Pyraminx from YJ Fest 2018.

Note: TNoodle contains a mechanism to contact the WCA website and detect if it is out of date, but this mechanism cannot detect if it is out of date when the computer is not connected to the internet (which is common at competitions). Individuals generating scrambles are reminded to take care and make sure they have the latest version of TNoodle on hand.

We know that this is a harsh decision that affects a significant number of competitors. However, the integrity of scrambles in WCA competitions is essential and the mission of the WCA states that we must strive for fair and equal conditions.

entries.title: 3x3x3 One-Handed Attempt was identified as misscramble
entries.content:
*DISCLAIMER*: Since the resolution of this incident, the regulation [11i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i) has been updated. The outcome of this incident wouldn't change, but how it should be handled is now explicitely stated in the regulations. 


A competitor broke the single World Record the first round of 3x3x3 One-Handed. It was later found that the cube was not scrambled correctly.

Original scramble: L2 D F2 D2 F2 L2 R2 D F U2 F' R' B2 F D' B2 L2 R'
Given scramble: L2 D F2 D2 F2 L2 R2 D F U2 F' R' B2 F D' B2 **L** R'

A provisional extra attempt was granted to the competitor. The WRC has decided to accept the result of the extra attempt as the official result because the given scramble was not an officially generated scramble.

Relevant Regulations:
[4b)](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b) Puzzles must be scrambled using computer-generated random scramble sequences.
[4g)](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4g) After scrambling a puzzle, the scrambler must verify that the puzzle is scrambled correctly. If the puzzle state is wrong, the scrambler must correct it (e.g. by solving the puzzle and applying the scramble sequence again).

This decision is in line with several precedents.

entries.title: Competitor made a move in the memorization phase of Multi Blind
entries.content:
During their Multi Blind attempt, a competitor accidentaly made a move on one of their cubes during the memorization phase.

Rule B3c) forbids to apply moves during the memorization (penalty : disqualification of the attempt), and is not superseded by other rules in the F article, so the whole attempt should be disqualified.

However, the WRC found more fair to consider only that cube as unsolved, and let the competitor continue the rest of the attempt.

entries.title: Scramblers made a consistent mistake in clock scrambling
entries.content:
In Clock finals, a competitor noticed while reconstructing their solves that every single pin was the opposite of what it should have been.

After investigation, it appeared that all scramblers had a misconception about pin scrambling, and made that mistake through the whole round. 

The WRC decided to keep the results of the round, since:
1. it was not the competitors' fault, and
2. in this specific case, the random distribution of scrambles states was consistently preserved by the mistake.
The scrambles in the database were updated to reflect the actual scrambles received by the competitors.

entries.title: Truncated Skewb scrambles in versions of TNoodle version 0.13.4 and earlier
entries.content:
A bug in TNoodle 0.13.4 and earlier resulted in 86 Skewb scrambles for official competitions that were accidentally truncated. As a result, they were not generated in a way that satisfies the requirements in [Regulation 4b3](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b3). Of these scrambles, 73 were for [CubingUSA Nationals 2018](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/competitions/CubingUSANationals2018/). The WRC has decided to keep these results.

As described in [the TNoodle 0.13.5 announcement](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/posts/tnoodle-0-13-5):

> Per the WCA Regulations, an official scramble sequence for Skewb must produce a random state ([4b3](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b3)) from those that require at least 7 moves ([4b3c](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b3c)) to solve.
> 
> In order to make it hard to distinguish scrambles with short solutions on a scramble sheet, TNoodle was designed to ensure that all generated Skewb scramble sequences are at least 11 moves (even if there is an optional solution with fewer moves). However, a thread safety bug in TNoodle before version `0.13.5` made it possible for scramble sequences to be truncated, such that:
> 
> * a truncated scramble sequence would be used if it required at least 7 moves to solve (still satisfying Regulation 4b3c), but
> * the truncation did not preserve the random scramble distribution (violating Regulation 4b3).
> 
> More details are available [at the TNoodle project on GitHub](https://github.com/thewca/tnoodle/pull/368).
> 
> An analysis of solution lengths for historical scrambles suggests that this did not affect the distribution of states for the vast majority of past competitions. However, it did result in a significant bias of states towards shorter optimal solutions for at least one major competition ([CubingUSA Nationals 2018](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/competitions/CubingUSANationals2018)), which led to the discovery of this bug. We would like to thank Sébastien Auroux for bringing it to our attention, and Tim Reynolds for working with Jeremy Fleischman to identify and prepare a fix for TNoodle over the past weekend.

We have also verified that scrambles for other puzzles were not affected by a bug like this.

A full list of affected scrambles is available [here](https://github.com/SAuroux/wca-analysis/blob/master/results-scripts/scramble_validity_analysis/skewb_outliers_20181005.txt). In particular, the distribution of optimal solution length for Skewb scrambles at CubingUSA Nationals 2018 was as follows:

| Optimal Solution Length | Expected # of scrambles | Actual # of scrambles |
|-------------------------|-------------------------|-----------------------|
| 7 moves                 | ≈20                     | 51                    |
| 8 moves                 | ≈78                     | 84                    |
| 9 moves                 | ≈93                     | 61                    |
| 10 moves                | ≈5                      | 0                     |
| 11 moves                | ≈0                      | 0                     |

We believe that the large number of attempts for the competition caused conditions for the bug to happen with higher likelihood on the computer that was used to generate scramble sequences for CubingUSA Nationals 2018.

Although the impact on the scramble distribution is measurable, the WRC has decided to keep all Skewb results from the 86 truncated scrambles because:

1. We do not believe that this bug was known to anyone, or purposely used by any organizers, Delegates, or competitors. This bug is the responsibility of the WRC and the WST.
2. Delegates properly followed the Regulations by using the output of a current official version TNoodle without inspecting or analyzing the scrambles ahead of time, as required by [Regulation 4b1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4b1).
3. The scrambles all still required at least of 7 moves for an optimal solution.
4. The affected results are not affected to the extent that the competitors received a clearly unfair advantage against future Skewb competitors.

For future incidents, please note that attempts should still be removed if their scramble sequences do not follow the Regulations because they did not come from a current official scramble program, as in the case of [an incident where an old version of TNoodle was used by accident](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/24).

entries.title: A competitor started his timer twice
entries.content:
After their inspection, a competitor started their timer, then reset it, then started it again before making any move.
Regulation [A4d](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A4d) states that the competitor starts the solve by removing their hands from the timer (thus starting the timer), which happened during the first time they started the timer.
Therefore the competitor reset the timer before the puzzle was solved and the result should be DNF.

For the case which occurred during China Championship 2017, the WRC also considered that the timer lights were covered by tape. However since it was the competitor's fifth solve on the exact same timer, the WRC decided to change the result to DNF.

entries.title: A judge forgot to hold a sheet between the competitor's face and the puzzle (extra not available)
entries.content:
A judge forgot to hold a sheet between the competitor's face and the puzzle. This was found after the end of the competition and no extra was granted.

The WRC decided to accept the result as the video showed no sign of the competitor abusing the situation and it was not his fault.

entries.title: Competition did not use proper covers for puzzles
entries.content:
Due to a miscommunication, Cavite Open 2 2018 did not have puzzle covers on hand. The organizers decided to use letter-sized paper and score sheets instead.

Video evidence confirms that significant portions of puzzles were visible to competitors and spectators before attempts. This violates Regulation A2c1:

> [A2c1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A2c1)) The scrambler places a cover over the scrambled puzzle that makes it impossible for any competitors or spectators to see any part of the puzzle. The cover remains over the puzzle until the start of the attempt.

In addition, Guideline A2c1+) explicitly clarifies that paper or score sheets are not an acceptable substitute:

> [A2c1+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/guidelines.html#A2c1+)) REMINDER In the past, score sheets have been used to cover puzzles while leaving some sides exposed. This is no longer permitted.

Although there is no evidence anyone specifically intended to cheat, this is a serious violation of scramble secrecy.
Per Motion [04.2019.1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/documents/motions/04.2019.1%20-%20Board%20of%20Directors.pdf) 2.8 and [Regulation 8f](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#8f), all results from Cavite Open 2 2018 have been removed.

entries.title: Incorrect Square-1 scramble (cube shape)
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since the resolution of this incident, the regulation [11i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i) has been updated. The outcome of this incident wouldn't change, but how it should be handled is now explicitely stated in the regulations.

At least one competitor received an incorrect Square-1 scramble which started with a "cube shape". Analysis shows that this provided the competitor a clear advantage for the attempt compared to any possible scramble for the attempt.

The WRC has concluded that such attempts should be disqualified, since:

1) Starting with cube shape provides a significant advantage for virtually all competitors (vs. receiving a scramble several moves away from cube shape).
2) This is a significant breach of scramble accountability. A qualified scrambler would never send out such a scramble by accident, since cube shape scrambles are conspicuously uncommon and a [check against the scramble image](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#4g) would have clearly shown that the scramble was incorrect.

entries.title: A competitor used headphones for Multi-Blind
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since resolution of this incident, the WRC has reconsidered it's stance on penalties given to competitors who received wrong information from a delegate. [This more recent incident](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/81) takes into account that more lenient stance in situations like this.

Due to a miscommunication, a WCA Delegate allowed a competitor to use unplugged headphones for his first two Multi-BLD attempts instead of earplugs/earmuffs.

This violates Regulation 2i):

> [2i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i)) While competing, competitors must not use electronics or audio equipment (e.g. cell phones, MP3 players, dictaphones, additional lighting) apart from the Stackmat timer or stopwatch.

In addition, Guideline 2i1b+) explicitly clarifies that switched off devices are not allowed:

> [2i1b+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/guidelines.html#2i1b+)) CLARIFICATION This includes relevant devices which are switched off or disconnected.

In addition, Regulation [2t](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2t)) requieres the competitor to be familiar with the Regulations. Therefore the WRC decision is to change the affected attempts into **DNF**.

entries.title: Pyraminx attempt was identified as misscramble
entries.content:
*DISCLAIMER:* Since the resolution of this incident, the regulation [11i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11i) has been updated. The outcome of this incident wouldn't change, but how it should be handled is now explicitely stated in the regulations. 


A competitor broke the Algerian National Record in the final round of Pyraminx. The WDC found out that the puzzle was not scrambled correctly and the misscrable was clearly easier than the official scramble. The competitor was granted a provisional extra attempt at the competition.

The WRC decided to replace the original attempt with the **extra** attempt.

entries.title: A competitor took a photo of his Fewest Moves solution sheet before giving it to the Delegate
entries.content:
A competitor briefly used his phone to take a photo of his Fewest Moves solution sheet just before giving it to the Delegate. Although the competitor didn't try to use it for cheating; it's a clear violation of regulation 2i).

> [2i](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i)) While competing, competitors must not use electronics or audio equipment (e.g. cell phones, MP3 players, dictaphones, additional lighting) apart from the Stackmat timer or stopwatch.

Therefore the WRC decision is to change the affected attempt into **DNF**.

entries.title: A competitor received another competitor's skewb and did not notice until the solve was done
entries.content:
A competitor was given the scoresheet and skewb of another competitor's due to the competitors having similar names. The competitor did not notice until after the solve was done, as the name on the scorecard did not match the competitor's. This competitor was given an Extra.

The WRC decided to replace the original attempt with the **extra** attempt.

entries.title: Two competitors attempted to help investigate a duplicate scramble situation
entries.content:
During 4x4 Blindfolded, a competitor claimed that a duplicate scramble is given. Two other competitors went to check the scramble at the solving station, which is something only the Delegate should do. The other two competitors saw the scramble, which they hadn't received yet. 

Although competitors must not attempt to gain information about future scrambles, it was clear in this situation that the competitors made a mistake in trying to be helpful, and were not attempting to cheat by trying to check the scramble.

The WRC decided to uphold the Delegate's decision, which was to generate **extra** scrambles for these competitors.

entries.title: Timer ran in slow mode
entries.content: A competitor set a time of 7.51 seconds. When checking the video of the solve, it was clear that the solve took more than 7 seconds. The timer was checked and it was found that the timer would stop for a while after lifting both hands. The timer was removed and an extra attempt was granted by the Delegate.

entries.title: A competitor was allowed to compete early in the 3×3×3 final and with different scrambles
entries.content:
A competitor who had made it to the 3×3×3 final asked that he do his average early, as the competitor had to leave for a flight. The WCA Delegates decided to accomodate his request as the competition wasn't running on time and the final was going to start well after it was scheduled to. While the second group of Megaminx was ongoing, the competitor did his average using the spare scrambles from 3×3×3 One Handed finals which had not been used.

Other competitors missed the final as they had to leave too, however the WCA Delegates weren't made aware of this until finals were underway and the competitors had already left. Due to absent competitors, the WCA Delegates asked anyone remaining in the top 20 to compete.

The Guideline 1h++) recommends to use the same scrambles for finals:

> [1h++](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/guidelines.html#1h++)) RECOMMENDATION All attempts in the final round of an event, as well as all 3x3x3 Fewest Moves attempts, should have the same scramble sequences for all competitors (i.e. only 1 group).

The WRC recommend to use the same scramble for finals (as cited before) and to warn all competitors that may need to leave the venue early if there is an opportunity to compete earlier. The WRC would also like to encourage competitors to reach out to the WCA Delegate in case they need to leave the venue early by justified causes.

As [TNoodle](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/scrambles/) generates 3×3×3 and 3×3×3 One Handed the same, the WRC decided to **allow all these attempts**.

entries.title: A competitor did several attempts with an illegal puzzle without accepting the extra attempts
entries.content:
A competitor competed with a cube where one of the stickers on the red face was a distinguishable shade from the others. This violates Regulation 3d2):

> [3d2](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3d2)) The colors of the colored parts must be solid, with one uniform color per face. Each color must be clearly distinct from the other colors.

The competitor did 4 attempts with this cube, and then did the last attempt with a legal cube. When the WCA Delegate asked if the competitor wanted to replace the 4 solves with extras (using Regulation [3k2a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3k2a)), the competitor declined.

As the round had a cutoff, the competitor did not make the cutoff after his first two solves (as stated by [11e2](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#11e2)), so the WRC has decided to record the results as DNS, DNS. Because all competitor's attempts are considered DNS, the competitor has not started any attempt. Therefore, the competitor's result should be removed.

entries.title: PVC coating on a stickerless cube
entries.content:
A competitor used a stickerless cube with a "PVC coating" on each colored part. The puzzle was accepted at the competition.

Similar cubes with non-transparent (black) stickers have previously been allowed, and the WRC has concluded that the PVC coatings do not give the competitor an advantage that [Regulation 3d](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3d)) and [Regulation 3h](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#3h)) are meant to prevent.

Therefore, the WRC has decided that it is reasonable for these puzzles to be permitted.

The WCA Regulations will be updated to clarify this.

entries.title: A competitor submitted a wrong number of puzzles for Multi-Blind
entries.content:
During Multi-BLD, a competitor submitted his puzzles to be scrambled, without writing down a declared number of cubes. The scramblers scrambled all the puzzles and wrote down it on the scorecard. When the competitor came to solve, he told the judge that he wanted to attempt a number of cubes lower than the amount submitted. The judge intended to give the competitor the amount that he said he wanted to attempt, but miscounted and gave the competitor the full amount of cubes that were sumbitted.

The WCA Delegate allowed the competitor to attempt the amount that he had claimed, rather than the amount that he had submitted. Due to the staff's mistake in counting the attempt, the delegate gave a provisional extra.

Although the competitor said a different number later, he initially submitted all the puzzles and did not mark anything on the scoresheet. This violates Regulation H1a):
> [H1a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#H1a)) Before an attempt, the competitor must submit to the organization team the number of puzzles (at least 2) they wish to attempt.

In addition, Regulation H1a1) explicitly clarifies that changing the number of puzzles is not allowed:
> [H1a1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#H1a1)) A competitor is not permitted to change the number of puzzles after submitting their number to the organization team.

Therefore, the WRC decision was to consider the total amount of cubes attempted as the original amount the competitor had submitted.

entries.title: A1c and 2i1 apply in Fewest Moves Solving
entries.content:
DISCLAIMER: Since this was brought to the WRC's attention, regulation [2k6](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/full/#2k6) has been created, which makes it required for competitors to fullfill the requirements  (e.g. knowing how to solve the puzzle) of all events they are competing in.

It was recently brought to the WRC's attention that [Regulation A1c](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A1c)) arguably does not apply to Fewest Moves under the current structure of the WCA Regulations, because Article E does not refer to Article A.

However, one of the original motivations for Regulation A1c) was to allow Delegates to apply it to Fewest Moves, and the WRC has supported this intended use of A1c since its introduction.

The Regulations will be updated to reflect this, as well as clarifying that the allowed aids specified under [Regulation 2i1](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#2i1)) are also allowed in Fewest Moves Solving.

entries.title: A competitor noticeably touched the puzzle immediately after stopping the timer
entries.content:
In Skewb, a competitor touched the puzzle immediately after stopping the timer. When releasing the puzzle, it fell into the lap of the competitor and then it jumped back to the mat.

This violates Regulation A6e):
> [A6e](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A6e)) After releasing the puzzle, the competitor must not touch or move the puzzle until the judge has inspected the puzzle. Penalty: disqualification of the attempt (DNF). Exception: If no moves have been applied, a time penalty (+2 seconds) may be assigned instead, at the discretion of the judge.

In addition, Guideline A6e+) explicitly clarifies that this case is considered touching the puzzle:
> [A6e+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/guidelines.html#A6e+)) CLARIFICATION If the puzzle falls into the lap of the competitor after stopping the timer, this is considered touching the puzzle.

By reviewing video evidences, the WRC determined that this case is not comparable with [this other](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/23) as the competitor in this incident noticeably touched the puzzle. The WRC concluded that it is appropriate to apply a **+2 penalty** to the affected attempt.

entries.title: A competitor claimed an incorrect result was written down on the score sheet
entries.content:
A competitor claimed a attempt's result was incorrectly written and requested a result change.
The only video evidence available was a live stream video, which did not show a readable time on the display or the timer.

The original time written on the score sheet was accepted, because the result was both signed by the judge and the competitor and there was no reliable video evidence to support the result change.

entries.title: An inproper room was used for Fewest Moves Solving
entries.content:
The Organization Team used a small room for Fewest Moves Solving for a large number of competitors. This caused competitors to be very close to each other. This could have been used by competitors to cheat and look off another competitor's paper. 

However, the WRC has decided to **accept** the results because:
1.  The WCA Delegates checked the solution sheets and saw that no competitors had the same solution.
2.  The WCA Delegates carefully oversaw the competitors during the round.
3.  There is no evidence that any competitors abused the situation to gain an unfair advantage.

entries.title: A competitor did not sign for an attempt and did not qualify for the finals
entries.content:
A competitor did not sign for an attempt in R2 and did not qualify for the final round. This was discovered after the competition. This violates Regulation A7c4:
> [A7c4](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7c4)) The competitor should not sign an attempt before the judge has recorded and signed the attempt. The competitor is ultimately responsible for ensuring that they and the judge have signed an attempt. If an attempt is found to be missing one or both signatures after the judge delivered the score sheet to the score taker (see [Regulation A7f](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A7f)), it will be considered unfinished (DNF).

Although the [Guideline A7c4+](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/guidelines.html#A7c4+) allows a competitor to add a missing signature if it is found by the score taker. The missing signature was found after the competition and thus, the guideline does not apply here.

The WRC agreed that the original attempt should be a **DNF** and therefore the attempts from the finals should be removed. In addition, there is an existing [Incident Log](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/19) that followed a similar reasoning.

More generally, this is what WRC decided to apply when results were wrongly entered, and someone mistakenly proceeded to the next round:

- Keep the results if the competitor proceeded thanks to an error in someone else's results
- Remove the results if the competitor proceeded thanks to an error in their own results

entries.title: The "Nod-don" technique was used for Blindfolded Solving
entries.content:
During 3x3 Blindfolded Round 2, a competitor was using the nod-don technique. Immediately after the solve, he informed the WCA Delegates that he thought it might be a bit close to starting the first turn before the blindfold was fully donned. The WCA Delegates granted a provisional extra before asking the WRC for feedback. This might violate Regulations B4a) and B4b):

> [B4a](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#B4a)) The competitor dons the blindfold to start the blindfolded phase.
> 
> [B4b](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#B4b)) The competitor must not apply moves to the puzzle before they have fully donned the blindfold. Penalty: disqualification of the attempt (DNF).

Since the video evidence was not enough to know if the don is legit or not, the WRC agreed to accept the provisional **extra** as the valid result.

entries.title: 3x3x3 Blindfolded solve without sight blocker
entries.content:
A judge did not use a sight blocker in a succesful solve. An extra attempt was granted just in case, but the Board decided that the original result should stand.

For an updated ruling on this type of cases please see this [Incident Log](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/incidents/21).

entries.title: A competitor stopped the timer with a "karate chop", only visible with video analysis
entries.content:
A competitor stopped the timer in a way that looked like it potentially violated the regulations (ie, with a "karate chop"). This violates Regulation A6d):

> [A6d](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/regulations/#A6d)) The competitor must stop the timer using both hands, placed flat on the sensors with palms down. Penalty: time penalty (+2 seconds).

However, after analyzing the video evidence, the WRC has concluded that the bad timer stop is only visible if the video was analyzed frame-by-frame. Therefore, the WRC agrees that the original time **should not be penalized**. The WRC is also proposed a new policy for delegates using video evidence to apply potential penalites to solves. 

**The WRC updated their approach on frame-by-frame analysis on September 27th, 2024, clarifying other use cases. Whilst this does not affect this previous decision, more information can be found [here](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/posts/wrc-decisions-with-frame-by-frame-analysis).**

entries.title: A tournament display showed a different result from the one recorded on the scorecard
entries.content:
During the competitions, results on the scorecards were found to not match the results on the tournament displays. This was found after both the competitor and the judge signed the attempt.
